Twentieth Century Practice
Although the profusion of administrative cases in the Twentieth 
Century comphcates generalizations, a representative case suggests the 
main thrust of the approach taken during this era. The very same year that 
the Court decided Crowell v. Benson, supra. Chief Justice Hughes alluded 
in a tax case to the “familiar principle . . . that great weight is attached to 
the construction consistently given to a statute by the executive 
dApartmAnt charged with its administration.” Burnet v. Chicago Portrait 
Co., 285 U.S. 1, 16 (1932). But the Court identified a “qualification of that 
principle” that was “as well established as the principle itself—namely, 
that the Court was “not bound by an administrative construction, and if 
that construction is not uniform and consistent, it will be taken into 
account only to the extent that it is supported by valid reasons.”
In the era immediately before the passage of the APA, the Court 
decided a series of cases that were to prove both controversial and 
influential. In Gray v. Powell, 314 U.S. 402 (1941), the Court reasoned that 
Congress had “delegate [d] th[e] function” of interpreting the statutory term 
“producer” “to those whose experience in a particular field gave promise of 
a better informed, more equitable” judgment. “To determine upon which 
side of the median line the particular instance falls,” the Court reasoned, 
“calls for the expert, experienced judgment of those familiar with the 
industry.” In Dobson v. Commissioner, 320 U.S. 489 (1943), the Court 
reasoned that in cases from the Tax Court, “when the Court cannot 
separate the elements of a decision so as to identify a clear-cut mistake of 
law, the decision of the Tax Court must stand,” and that “[i]n deciding law 
questions courts may properly attach weight to the decision of points of law 
by an administrative body having special competence to deal with the 
subject matter.” And in NLRB v. Hearst Publications, Inc., 322 U.S. Ill 
(1944), the Court reasoned that “where the question is one of specific
